suggestions.assertion: SUMMARY.md nomeia explicitamente pelo menos um token/animação/classe já existente que foi reusado
suggestions.reason: This assertion has a low bar — an agent could satisfy it by merely name-dropping an existing token in prose without actually reusing it correctly in code (e.g. mention `--bus-red` in the writeup while still hardcoding a hex value in the diff). It passed here with strong, verified evidence (the named tokens genuinely appear reused correctly in changes.diff), but the assertion itself doesn't cross-check the SUMMARY.md claim against the diff. A stronger version would require that at least one specifically named token/class in SUMMARY.md also appears reused (not just declared) in changes.diff.

No assertion checks that the changed component still respects the file's existing data-guard patterns (e.g. the ETA badge's live-pulse-vs-static-icon branch only firing when `getEtaTier !== 'none'`, so it doesn't visually claim live data that isn't there). This was a genuinely good piece of restraint the agent exercised (per SUMMARY.md and confirmed in the diff) that no assertion rewards or would catch if it were missing — worth considering for a future 'doesn't overclaim data it doesn't have' type of assertion in UI-polish evals, since that's exactly the kind of shortcut a lower-quality agent would take (always showing the pulse for visual flair) and that a token-reuse-only assertion set wouldn't catch.

eval_feedback.overall: All 5 assertions passed with strong, independently-verified evidence (not just surface compliance — I cross-checked every named token/keyframe/function against the actual current repo files, not just trusted SUMMARY.md's prose, and grepped the diff itself for any smuggled-in hex/rgba literals). The assertion set is well-targeted at this skill's specific failure mode (introducing new colors/motion instead of reusing the existing design system) and is genuinely discriminating — a lazy or careless agent would very plausibly have hardcoded a new red/violet shade or used a generic linear fade, and the assertions would have caught that. The main caveat is the missing transcript, which limits confidence in process claims (e.g., whether the skill was actually invoked, whether the audit genuinely preceded the edits) to what SUMMARY.md self-reports.

eval_critique: The assertion set is tightly scoped to this skill's core value proposition (design-system discipline: reuse tokens/animations, don't invent near-duplicate colors, use non-linear motion) and each one is discriminating in practice — I verified independently against the real repo (not just trusting the transcript/SUMMARY.md) that every named token, keyframe, and function genuinely pre-existed, and that zero new color literals were introduced anywhere in the diff, which is a meaningfully hard bar to clear by accident. The weakest assertion is the SUMMARY.md-naming one, since it only checks that a name is mentioned in prose, not that the mentioned thing is actually reused correctly in code — it happened to hold up here under independent scrutiny, but a future eval could tighten it to require the named token/class to also appear in changes.diff. The biggest process gap is external to the eval definition: the transcript file was empty, which blocks verification of any process-level expectation (ordering of skill invocation, audit-before-edit, etc.); this eval's assertions didn't happen to need that, but the eval harness losing transcripts silently (0-byte file rather than an error) is worth flagging separately from the assertion quality itself.
